In [[set theory]], a mathematical discipline, a '''fundamental sequence''' is a [[cofinal (mathematics)|cofinal]] [[sequence]] of [[Transfinite ordinal|ordinals]] all below a given [[limit ordinal]]. Depending on author, fundamental sequences may be restricted to ω-sequences only<ref name="RathjenArt">M. Rathjen, [https://www1.maths.leeds.ac.uk/~rathjen/ICMend.pdf The Art of Ordinal Analysis] (2006), pp. 9–10. Accessed 8 May 2023.</ref> or permit fundamental sequences of length [[First uncountable ordinal|<math>\mathrm{\omega}_1</math>]].<ref name="Buchholz15">W. Buchholz, [https://www.mathematik.uni-muenchen.de/~buchholz/articles/jaegerfestschr_buchholz3.pdf A survey on ordinal notations around the Bachmann-Howard ordinal] (2017), p.2. Accessed 8 May 2023.</ref> The <math>n^{\text{th}}</math> element of the fundamental sequence of <math>\alpha</math> is commonly denoted <math>\alpha[n]</math>,<ref name="Buchholz15" /> although it may be denoted <math>\alpha_n</math><ref name="BuchholzWainer87">W. Buchholz, S. Wainer, [https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/3843/1/3843.pdf Provably Computable Functions and the Fast Growing Hierarchy] (1987), Contemporary Mathematics, vol. 65 (pp. 180–181).</ref> or <math>\{\alpha\}(n)</math>.<ref name="FreundPakhomov20">A. Freund, F. Pakhomov, [https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.03251v2 Short Proofs for Slow Consistency] (2020). Accessed 8 May 2023.</ref> Additionally, some authors may allow fundamental sequences to be defined on [[successor ordinal]]s.<ref name="BCW94">W. Buchholz, A. Cichon, A. Weiermann, [https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/3849/1/16.pdf A Uniform Approach to Fundamental Sequences and Hierarchies] (1994), Mathematical Logic Quarterly, vol. 40, pp.273–285.</ref> The term dates back to (at the latest) [[Veblen function|Veblen's construction]] of [[normal function]]s <math>\varphi_\alpha</math>, while the concept dates back to [[G. H. Hardy|Hardy]]'s 1904 attempt to construct a set of [[cardinality]] <math>\aleph_1</math>.<ref>[[Oswald Veblen|O. Veblen]], [https://www.ams.org/journals/tran/1908-009-03/S0002-9947-1908-1500814-9/S0002-9947-1908-1500814-9.pdf Continuous Increasing Functions of Finite and Transfinite Ordinals] (1908).</ref>

==Definition==
Given an ordinal <math>\alpha</math>, a '''fundamental sequence''' for <math>\alpha</math> is a sequence <math>(\alpha[n])_{n\in\mathbb N}</math> such that <math>\forall(n\in\mathbb N)(\alpha[n]<\alpha)</math> and <math>\textrm{sup}\{\alpha[n]\mid n\in\mathbb N\}=\alpha</math>.<ref name="RathjenArt" /> An additional restriction may be that the sequence of ordinals must be [[strictly increasing]].<ref name="PTV91">H. J. Prömel, W. Thumser, B. Voigt, "[https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0012365X91903464 Fast growing functions and Ramsey theorems]" (1991), [[Discrete Mathematics (journal)|Discrete Mathematics]] vol. 95, pp. 341–358.</ref>

==Examples==
The following is a common assignment of fundamental sequences to all limit ordinals less than [[epsilon number|<math>\varepsilon_0</math>]].<ref name="Weiermann06">A. Weiermann, [https://www.jstor.org/stable/4617258 Classifying the Provably Total Functions of PA] (2006), [[Bulletin of Symbolic Logic]] vol. 12 no. 2, pp. 177–190.</ref><ref name="FreundPakhomov20" /><ref name="BuchholzWainer87" />
*<math>\omega^{\alpha+1}[n]=\omega^\alpha\cdot(n+1)</math>
*<math>\omega^\alpha[n]=\omega^{\alpha[n]}</math> for limit ordinals <math>\alpha</math>
*<math>(\omega^{\alpha_1}+\ldots+\omega^{\alpha_k})[n]=\omega^{\alpha_1}+\ldots+(\omega^{\alpha_k}[n])</math> for <math>\alpha_1 \geq \dots \geq \alpha_k</math>.
This is very similar to the system used in the [[Fast-growing hierarchy#The Wainer hierarchy|Wainer hierarchy]].<ref name="PTV91" />

==Usage==
Fundamental sequences arise in some settings of definitions of [[large countable ordinal]]s, definitions of [[fast-growing hierarchy|hierarchies of fast-growing functions]], and [[proof theory]]. [[Heinz Bachmann|Bachmann]] defined a hierarchy of functions <math>\phi_\alpha</math> in 1950, providing a system of names for ordinals up to what is now known as the [[Bachmann–Howard ordinal]], by defining fundamental sequences for namable ordinals below <math>\omega_1</math>.<ref>J. Bridge, [https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/2271898.pdf A Simplification of the Bachmann Method for Generating Large Countable Ordinals]</ref> This system was subsequently simplified by [[Solomon Feferman|Feferman]] and [[Peter Aczel|Aczel]] to reduce the reliance on fundamental sequences.<ref>S. Feferman, [https://math.stanford.edu/~feferman/papers/id-saga.pdf The proof theory of classical and constructive inductive definitions. A 40 year saga, 1968-2008.] (2008). Accessed 8 May 2023.</ref>

The [[fast-growing hierarchy]], [[Hardy hierarchy]], and [[slow-growing hierarchy]] of functions are all defined via a chosen system of fundamental sequences up to a given ordinal. The fast-growing hierarchy is closely related to the Hardy hierarchy, which is used in proof theory along with the slow-growing hierarchy to majorize the provably [[computable function]]s of a given theory.<ref name="Weiermann06" /><ref>T. Arai, [https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/81193193.pdf A slow-growing analogue to Buchholz's proof] (1991), [[Annals of Pure and Applied Logic]] vol. 54, pp. 101–120.</ref> Fundamental sequences also have applications in [[computability theory]] and the [[Turing jump]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lubarsky |first=Robert S. |date=December 1987 |title=Uncountable master codes and the jump hierarchy |journal=The Journal of Symbolic Logic |volume=52 |issue=4 |pages=952–958 |doi=10.2307/2273829 |issn=0022-4812 |jstor=2273829 |s2cid=46113113}}</ref>

===Additional conditions===
A system of fundamental sequences up to <math>\alpha</math> is said to have the '''Bachmann property''' if for all ordinals <math>\alpha,\beta</math> in the domain of the system and for all <math>n\in\mathbb N</math>, <math>\alpha[n]<\beta<\alpha\implies\alpha[n]<\beta[0]</math>. If a system of fundamental sequences has the Bachmann property, all the functions in its associated fast-growing hierarchy are monotone, and <math>f_\beta</math> eventually dominates <math>f_\alpha</math> when <math>\alpha<\beta</math>.<ref name="PTV91" />
